micromouse 4wd · aero study

Air is not what is slowing your mouse down

At 5 m/s the whole robot pushes 28.7 mN of air — about 1.33 % of its own weight, and less than the friction of its own tyres rolling. Below 2 m/s it is close to unmeasurable. This page computes that from the real CAD silhouette rather than a guess, and shows what the flow actually does in straights and in corners.

Drag versus speed

Drag grows with the square of speed, so it is negligible at 1 m/s (1.15 mN) and still small at 5 m/s. The band is the honest uncertainty in Cd for a bluff, open-wheeled, ground-proximity body (0.70–1.15); the line is Cd 0.90. The dashed line is rolling resistance — drag only catches it at 5.31 m/s.

aero drag (band = Cd 0.70–1.15) rolling resistance (Crr 0.015)

Where it sits in the force budget

The comparison that settles it: at full speed, drag is roughly a hundredth of the grip the tyres can deliver. Nothing about the robot's lap time is decided by air.

Straights and corners

In a corner the body runs at a slip angle, so it presents a slightly bigger area and picks up a side force. The slip angles here are not assumed — they are measured in sim_twin, the same offline twin that tunes the controller: 2.3° mean in corners at 0.8 m/s, 6.7° at the 95th percentile at 3 m/s. That attitude adds only 8.5 % to the frontal area, and the side force at 5 m/s is 5.23 mN — three orders of magnitude below the cornering force the tyres are already carrying.

5 m/s through a corner is not physically reachable on this robot: a 90 mm turn radius on race-glue tyres caps corner speed near 1.19 m/s on grip alone. The cornering column is the drag the robot would see at that attitude, listed at the same speeds so the comparison is like-for-like.

What the flow does

A 2D lattice-Boltzmann solve over the robot's real silhouette. Read these for the shape of the wake, not for a number: the lattice runs near Re 10³ while the robot at 5 m/s is at Re 39,578, so the separation points are indicative and the turbulent detail is not resolved. Every force on this page comes from the drag equation, never from these fields.

So what would actually help

Nothing aerodynamic — at this scale streamlining buys back a fraction of a milliNewton. The forces that decide your lap time are grip (tyre compound and how much of the friction circle the planner dares to use), motor back-EMF ceiling, and mass. The one aero effect worth remembering is the opposite of drag: at these speeds you get essentially no downforce either, which is why the full-size mice that chase 2 m/s corner speeds fit a vacuum fan and generate their own.

Frontal, side and plan areas rasterised at 0.5 mm from the tessellated assembly (Gear/aero_study.py); slip angles logged from sim_twin.py; flow fields from a D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann solver over the same silhouettes (Gear/aero_flow.py). Air at 20 °C (ρ 1.204 kg/m³, ν 1.516×10⁻⁵ m²/s), robot mass 0.22 kg. Cd band and Crr are literature values for bluff ground vehicles, not measurements — they are the least certain inputs here, and the conclusion holds across the whole band.
